blocks.md:
- Explain what a ledger line is and why it exists.
- Find and name any note that sits on or between one ledger line above or below the treble or bass stave.
- Locate middle C on the piano and read it correctly in both the treble and bass clefs.
blocks.label: In this lesson

blocks.md: Every note you read on a stave sits either on a line or in a space between two lines. The stave (the grid of lines that music is written on) has exactly five lines. That works well for the notes in the middle of the piano. But music uses many more notes than those five lines can hold. Some notes are higher. Some are lower. So what happens when a note does not fit on the stave?

The answer is a **ledger line**. A ledger line is a short, extra line that is added just for one note, sitting above or below the stave. Think of it like a small extension that appears only when it is needed, then disappears again. It does not change the stave itself. It is simply a small extension, added for that single note.
**Ledger line:** a short extra line added above or below the stave to show a note that is too high or too low to fit on the five main lines.
Here is what a normal five-line stave looks like, with no notes on it yet.

blocks.caption: A plain five-line stave. There are exactly five lines and four spaces between them.

blocks.md: Now look at the note below. It sits on a small line of its own, floating just below the stave. That small line is a ledger line. The note is too low to sit on any of the five main lines, so we add an extra line.

blocks.caption: Middle C written in the treble clef. It sits on one ledger line just below the stave.

blocks.md: You can also have a note sitting above the stave on a ledger line, or even in the space just above or below a ledger line.

Ledger lines follow the exact same rules as the five main lines. The note names still go A, B, C, D, E, F, G and then start again. Nothing new to learn about the letters. You are simply moving a little further up or down the same musical ladder.

In the treble clef, the top line of the stave is F. Go one space up and you reach G. Go one more step and you land on A, sitting on its own ledger line above the stave. The ledger line is short and sits right through the middle of the note head, just like the five main lines do for notes on those lines.
blocks.title: A note on a ledger line above the stave

blocks.caption: G sits above the treble stave. A sits in the first ledger line above the stave.

blocks.md: The ledger line is always just on that individual note. It is never as long as the full stave lines. That short length is what makes it easy to spot: if you see a small line, you know it is a ledger line.

The most important thing to remember at this stage is this: ledger lines are not scary. They are just the stave continuing, a little bit at a time, in whichever direction the music needs to go. You already know how to count up and down the musical alphabet. Ledger lines simply ask you to keep counting a little further.

items.prompt: How many lines does a standard musical stave have?
items.explain: A stave always has exactly five lines. Ledger lines are extras added outside those five when a note is too high or too low to fit.

items.prompt: A ledger line is a long extra line that is added permanently to make the stave bigger.
items.explain: A ledger line is short and appears only for the note that needs it. It is a tiny extension, not a permanent part of the stave.

items.prompt: Do notes on ledger lines use different letter names from notes on the main stave?
items.explain: Notes always use the same seven letter names: A, B, C, D, E, F, and G. Ledger lines simply extend the stave; the naming rules do not change.
options: Yes, ledger line notes have special names
No, they use the same A to G letter names as all other notes
Only the ledger lines above the stave use different names

blocks.text: Middle C: The Ledger Note You Already Know

blocks.md: You met middle C in the last lesson, so here is a quick reminder before we go further. Middle C is the most common ledger-line note of all. It sits just outside both staves on its own short ledger line, and it is the note that links the treble and bass clefs together.
In the **treble clef**, middle C sits on one ledger line just **below** the stave.
In the **bass clef**, the very same key sits on one ledger line just **above** the stave.

One ledger line below the treble stave, or one ledger line above the bass stave, is middle C. Same key, two staves. On the grand stave it sits in the gap between the two staves, which is why it is called the bridge between the clefs.

blocks.abc:
X:1
L:1/4
K:C
[V:1 clef=treble] C4
[V:2 clef=bass] C4

items.prompt: In the bass clef, where does middle C sit?
items.explain: In the bass clef, middle C sits on a single ledger line just above the stave. It mirrors where it appears in the treble clef, but on the opposite side of its stave.
options: On a ledger line just below the stave
On the top line of the stave
On a ledger line just above the stave
In the top space of the stave

items.prompt: When you play middle C from a treble clef version and then from a bass clef version, you press two different keys on the piano.
items.explain: Middle C is always the same key, no matter which clef it is written in. The notation looks different, but the pitch and the key you press are identical.

blocks.text: The Treble Stave: One Line Above

blocks.md: Every time a note climbs higher than the space above the treble stave, we add a short ledger line to give it somewhere to sit or to pass through.

Let's look at three notes that live just above the treble stave. They are G, A, and B, and they sit very close together. The key is to notice that spaces exist around a ledger line, just as spaces exist between the five main lines of the stave.

**Lines and spaces always take turns.** On the stave, a line is followed by a space, then a line, then a space. The same pattern continues above (and below) the stave with ledger lines. A ledger line has one space just below it and one space just above it.

blocks.text: The Three Notes: G, A, and B

blocks.md: Here is how the three notes are arranged:

- **G** sits in the space just below the ledger line. It has floated off the top of the stave but has not yet reached the ledger line itself.
- **A** sits right on the ledger line. The line passes through the middle of the note head, just as a stave line passes through any note that sits on a line.
- **B** sits in the space just above the ledger line. It has risen above the ledger line and floats in the space above it.

blocks.abc:
X:1
L:1/4
K:C
[V:1 clef=treble] g4 a4 b4
blocks.caption: Left to right: G above the stave (space below the ledger line), A above the stave (on the ledger line), B above the stave (space above the ledger line). Notice how the single ledger line appears only for A.

blocks.md: Look at the notation above carefully. The ledger line only appears when the note needs it, that is, for A. For G, the note floats in the space below and needs no ledger line yet. For B, the note floats in the space above, and the ledger line still shows so your eye can track the position.

blocks.text: Where These Notes Sit on the Piano

blocks.md: These three notes are the G, A, and B that come after the E and F at the top of the treble stave's comfortable range. They are quite high and bright sounding.

blocks.label: G, A, and B above the treble stave

blocks.md: All three are white keys. They follow one another with no gaps, just like any three neighbouring white keys on the piano.

blocks.label: G, A, B above the stave played in order

blocks.md:
Sit at the piano and find the group of three black keys nearest to middle C, to the left of those notes is F on the keyboard. Now jump up to the next F (also to the left of the 3 three black keys) The white key just to the right of that group is G and to the right of that is A. That is the A we have been looking at, written on the ledger line above the treble stave.

1. Play that A with your right hand.
2. Now play the G just to its left.
3. Now play the B just to its right.

Say the note name out loud each time you play it. This links the key, the sound, and the name together.

items.prompt: Which note sits directly on the ledger line that appears one line above the treble stave?
items.explain: A sits on the ledger line itself. G is in the space just below that line, and B is in the space just above it.

items.prompt: There is a space just below the ledger line above the treble stave, and a space just above it. Both spaces can hold a note.
items.explain: Correct. Every ledger line has a space on each side of it, just as every line on the main stave does. G sits in the space below and B sits in the space above.

items.prompt: You are reading a treble clef piece and you see a note floating in the space above a single ledger line above the stave. Which note is it?
items.explain: The space above the ledger line is B. A sits on the ledger line, and G sits in the space below it.

blocks.text: Below the Bass Stave: F, E, D

blocks.md: The bass stave works exactly like the treble stave. When a note drops too low to sit on the five lines, we add a short ledger line just beneath the stave. Let's meet the three notes around that first ledger line below the bass stave.
Lines and spaces always take turns. The first ledger line below the bass stave has a space just above it (between the ledger line and the stave) and a space just below it. Each can hold a note.

blocks.text: The Three Notes: F, E, and D

blocks.md:
- **F** sits in the space just below the bottom line of the bass stave. It has dropped off the bottom of the stave but has not yet reached the ledger line.
- **E** sits right on the first ledger line below the stave. The line passes through the middle of the note head.
- **D** sits in the space just below the ledger line, one step lower than E.

blocks.abc:
X:1
L:1/4
K:C clef=bass
F,, E,, D,,

blocks.md: The ledger line appears for E, the note that sits on it. F floats in the space just above the ledger line (still below the stave), and D floats in the space just below it.

blocks.text: Where These Notes Sit on the Piano

blocks.md: These three notes sit well to the left of middle C, in the lower range your left hand plays. They are all white keys, one after another.

blocks.label: F, E, and D below the bass stave

blocks.md:
Sit at the piano and find these three low notes with your left hand.

1. Play **E** (on the ledger line).
2. Move one white key down to **D** (the space just below the ledger line).
3. Move up two white keys to **F** (the space just below the bottom line of the stave).

items.prompt: A note is written sitting directly on the first ledger line below the bass stave. What note is it?
items.explain: The bottom line of the bass stave is G. The space below it is F, and the first ledger line below is E.

items.prompt: Where does F sit in relation to that ledger line?
items.explain: F sits in the space just below the bottom line of the stave, which is the space just above the E ledger line.
options: In the space just above the ledger line (between it and the stave)

items.prompt: Of the three notes D, E and F below the bass stave, D is the lowest in pitch.
items.explain: D sits below the ledger line, lower than E (on the line) and F (above the line).

blocks.md: You can now read the notes on and around one ledger line above and below each stave. Look at the notation, say the name, then find and play the key.

**The notes you can now read:**

- **Middle C:** one ledger line below the treble stave, and one ledger line above the bass stave. Same key, two staves.
- **Above the treble stave:** G in the space above the top line, A on the ledger line, B in the space above it.
- **Below the bass stave:** F in the space below the bottom line, E on the ledger line, D in the space below it.

Ledger lines appear constantly in real piano music because the piano has a huge range, far wider than two staves alone can cover. The very first note that joins the treble and bass clef worlds, middle C, sits on a ledger line. As soon as you open almost any beginner piano piece you will see it sitting there on that short extra line, right in the middle of the grand stave. Spotting ledger lines quickly is one of the most practical reading skills you can build, and you have already made a strong start.

- **stave**: the set of five horizontal lines on which music is written
- **ledger line**: a short extra line added above or below a stave to show notes that are too high or too low to fit on the five main lines
- **treble clef**: the curly symbol at the start of the upper stave, used mainly for higher notes played by the right hand
- **bass clef**: the symbol at the start of the lower stave, used mainly for lower notes played by the left hand
- **grand stave**: the treble stave and bass stave joined together, which is how most piano music is written
- **middle C**: the C nearest the middle of the piano keyboard; it sits on its own ledger line between the treble and bass staves and is the note that connects both clefs

- A ledger line is a short extra line that extends the stave up or down for notes outside the five main lines.
- In the treble clef, one ledger line below the stave is middle C; one ledger line above the stave is A (A5).
- In the bass clef, one ledger line above the stave is middle C; one ledger line below the stave is E (E2).
- Middle C is the most important ledger-line note: it sits between the two staves on the grand stave and acts as a bridge between the treble and bass clefs.
- To read any ledger-line note, count from the nearest stave line, line then space then line, and the musical alphabet keeps going.

items.explain: A ledger line is a short extra line added above or below the stave when a note is too high or too low to sit on the stave's five main lines. It is not a bar line, and it is not part of the stave itself.
options: A line drawn through the middle of a note head to make it easier to read
A short extra line added above or below a stave to write notes that go beyond the stave's five lines
Another name for the top line of the treble stave
A line that separates one bar from the next

items.prompt: Middle C is written on one ledger line below the treble stave.
items.explain: Middle C sits on a single ledger line just below the treble stave. That same note can also be written on one ledger line just above the bass stave, which is why it acts as a bridge between the two clefs.

items.prompt: A note written on one ledger line above the treble stave is which note?
items.explain: The note on one ledger line above the treble stave is A. The top line of the treble stave is F, the space above it is G, and the first ledger line above is A. High C (C5) sits two ledger lines higher.

items.prompt: Middle C can be written using a ledger line in two different places. Name both clefs where this happens.
items.explain: Middle C is written on one ledger line below the treble stave and on one ledger line above the bass stave. This shared note is what links the two clefs together.

items.prompt: A note written one ledger line below the bass stave is D.
items.explain: The note on one ledger line below the bass stave is E. The bottom line of the bass stave is G, the space below it is F, and the first ledger line below is E. D is one step lower, in the space just below that ledger line.
